soil-found-082.title: Soil reclamation: rebuilding ground after disturbance
soil-found-082.text:
A disturbed site cannot simply be seeded and left. Soil reclamation is the part of land reclamation that rebuilds soil, usually after infrastructure removal, recontouring and contaminant cleanup and before revegetation. Land reclamation converts disturbed or damaged land to its former or another productive use, and covers soils, hydrology, flora and fauna. Soil reclamation and soil remediation are components of it. The goals depend on the end land use. Regulatory requirements are stricter for agricultural land and land people will occupy than for industrial land, and the end use may mean a different ecosystem.

Stripped {{ref:soil-found-077}} is normally replaced in its natural horizon sequence. Careful placement limits horizon mixing, and compaction on replacement can be eased by tillage. Damage is reduced by working under frozen or dry conditions, and soil quality is kept if stockpiles are held only briefly. Bare reclaimed soil is exposed to wind and water erosion, as in {{ref:soil-water-001}}, so contouring, amendments, erosion control blankets, mulch and bioengineering such as live staking are used.

Clay can be part of the fix. Soils rich in swelling smectite clays, a type of {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, are often very fertile: the smectite-rich paddy soils of Thailand's Central Plains are among the world's most productive. On low-clay soils in Thailand, adding bentonite clay once at 200 kilograms per rai (1,300 kg/ha) raised yields by an average of 73% in field trials. Soils too high in clay or salts can be balanced with gypsum, washed river sand and organic matter. Sandy, nutrient-poor soils benefit from compost or ramial chipped wood.

soil-env-314.title: Amendments that make reclaimed soil fit for use
soil-env-314.text:
A rebuilt soil rarely matches what its new land use demands. Amendments are the materials added to correct chemical, physical or biological properties, as part of {{ref:soil-found-082}}. Lack of organic matter is common and is fixed with animal manure, straw, or forest floor (LFH) material from a cleared area. Lack of nutrients is fixed with commercial nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium fertilizer blended for the site.

Waste materials are widely used, which also keeps them out of landfills. Raw sewage supplies nutrients and organic matter but may carry salts, metals and disease organisms. Biosolids, sewage sludges treated to lower pathogen risk, are widely used. Others include calcium sources, paper mill waste, industrial sludge, biochar and wood ash. Each has properties that suit a soil need and usually a drawback to balance, and many jurisdictions regulate waste use. Micro-topography such as mounds, furrows, depressions, rocks and mulches gives micro sites for plants and microbes and reduces erosion.

soil-hist-147.title: Photosynthesis: how light becomes the food that feeds soil
soil-hist-147.text:
Every sugar in a plant, and so nearly every scrap of organic matter in soil, began as light. Photosynthesis is the biological process by which plants, algae and cyanobacteria convert light energy into chemical energy stored in organic compounds. Usually the term means oxygenic photosynthesis, which splits water and releases oxygen. The stored carbohydrates are later used in cellular respiration, a reaction type that {{ref:soil-chem-113}} describes.

In plants, chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs red and blue light. The light reactions make NADPH and ATP, and the Calvin cycle then builds sugars from atmospheric CO2.

The scale is planetary. Photosynthesis maintains atmospheric oxygen and supplies most biological energy. Globally it captures about 130 terawatts and fixes 100-115 billion tons of carbon into biomass yearly. Individual plants are less impressive. They convert light with an efficiency usually of 3-6%, ranging from 0.1% to 8% with light, temperature and CO2.

The process was long misunderstood. In 1779 Jan Ingenhousz showed that plants need light, not just soil and water.

soil-hist-153.title: When photosynthesis began, and how it changed the air
soil-hist-153.text: Photosynthesis is older than oxygen in the air. It began early in Earth's history, probably as anoxygenic forms using hydrogen or sulfur rather than water. Possible filamentous photosynthetic fossils are 3.4 billion years old, and thylakoid membranes are preserved in 1.75-billion-year-old cherts. Using water as the electron source, the step that defines {{ref:soil-hist-147}} and depends on {{ref:soil-chem-113}}, evolved once, in a common ancestor of living cyanobacteria at least 2450-2320 million years ago. Their oxygen oxygenated Earth, an event sometimes called the oxygen catastrophe.

soil-hist-152.title: What limits how fast plants photosynthesize
soil-hist-152.text: Photosynthesis has a speed limit, and many things can set it. It is limited by light, by leaf area for capturing light, by CO2 supply to chloroplasts, by water and by temperature. Shading by other plants is a major limitation. Sugar production rises with CO2 concentration until another factor limits it. This is the pace of {{ref:soil-hist-147}}, and the electron transfers behind it are {{ref:soil-chem-113}}.

soil-hist-148.title: Light reactions: capturing sunlight as ATP and NADPH
soil-hist-148.text: The first stage of {{ref:soil-hist-147}} happens in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts. Chlorophyll absorbs light, and an electron passes through pheophytin and an electron transport chain to reduce NADP to NADPH. A proton gradient meanwhile drives ATP synthase. This is a chain of {{ref:soil-chem-113}}. Chlorophyll regains its lost electron when water is split by photolysis, releasing oxygen. Not all wavelengths work. In green plants the action spectrum peaks in violet-blue and red light, while red algae use blue-green light to grow deeper.

soil-hist-149.title: The Calvin cycle: building sugar from air
soil-hist-149.text: The second stage of {{ref:soil-hist-147}} needs no light directly, only the products of {{ref:soil-hist-148}}. RuBisCO captures CO2 and, using NADPH, makes three-carbon sugars. Those intermediates are combined into sucrose and starch. The sugars then feed cellulose, lipid and amino acid synthesis, or respiration. Reducing CO2 this way is {{ref:soil-chem-113}} at work.

soil-hist-150.title: Photorespiration: when RuBisCO grabs the wrong molecule
soil-hist-150.text: RuBisCO sometimes makes a costly mistake. When CO2 is low, it binds oxygen instead, in a wasteful process that uses energy and makes no sugar. The oxygen reaction yields phosphoglycolate, which the {{ref:soil-hist-149}} cannot use, and glycolate, which is toxic at high concentration and inhibits photosynthesis. Salvaging glycolate is energetically expensive: only 75% of its carbon returns to the cycle, and ammonia is lost, so nitrogen leaves the plant. Hot, dry conditions make it worse. Closed stomata drop CO2 and raise oxygen, increasing photorespiration. The oxygen involved is part of {{ref:soil-chem-113}}.

soil-hist-151.title: C4 and CAM: two ways to dodge photorespiration
soil-hist-151.text: Some plants have fixed the problem of {{ref:soil-hist-150}} by raising CO2 concentration at RuBisCO using PEP carboxylase. C4 plants separate the steps in space; CAM plants separate them in time. C4 plants fix CO2 in mesophyll cells into oxaloacetate, then release it in bundle sheath cells. There RuBisCO sits away from the oxygen-producing light reactions, which cuts photorespiration. They outproduce C3 plants in high light and temperature and include maize, sorghum, sugarcane and millet. Over 90% of plants are C3 and about 3% C4, yet C4 evolved in over sixty lineages. CAM plants such as cacti and succulents fix CO2 at night with open stomata, store it as malic acid and release it by day. About 16,000 species use it. All of this rests on {{ref:soil-chem-113}}.

soil-hist-146.title: Marine isotope stages: numbering ice ages
soil-hist-146.text:
Deep-sea mud keeps a record of ice ages. Marine isotope stages are the alternating warm and cool periods of Earth's climate deduced from oxygen isotope data in cores, as in {{ref:soil-found-117}}. Counting back from the present (MIS 1), even-numbered stages have high oxygen-18 and are cold glacials, while odd-numbered stages are warm interglacials.

The scale grew from Emiliani's 1950s work on Urey's prediction that the oxygen-18 ratio in {{ref:soil-found-118}} varies with water temperature. Shackleton showed in 1967 that ice-sheet volume was the main cause. The record matches Milankovitch orbital cycles, which helped that theory win acceptance, and it is the standard for correlating Quaternary climate records. Over 100 stages are identified. MIS 5e (about 123 kya) is the Last Interglacial, MIS 5d to 2 is the Last Glacial Period, and the list reaches MIS 104 at 2.614 million years ago.

soil-hist-145.title: Clumped isotopes: a thermometer inside carbonate
soil-hist-145.text:
Some rocks carry their own thermometer. Clumped isotopes are heavy isotopes bonded to other heavy isotopes within a molecule such as carbonate, and their abundance depends on temperature. The carbonate thermometer uses the temperature dependence of 13C-18O bonding in the lattice, with more clumping as temperature falls, reported as Δ47. Unlike conventional δ18O analysis it does not need the water's δ18O, so it gives temperature and lets source-water δ18O be reconstructed.

Carbonate is reacted with phosphoric acid to release CO2, which is purified and analyzed by mass spectrometry at precision near 10^-5. Uses include past lake and seawater temperatures, paleoaltimetry such as Andes uplift, and extinct animal body temperatures. The catch is that the signal is subtle (-0.0005%/°C) and the key isotopologue is about 60 ppm. Analyses take 2-3 hours and need large, uncontaminated samples.

soil-hist-144.title: OPAL Soil Centre and its earthworm survey
soil-hist-144.text: In March 2009, members of the public across England began digging up soil and counting worms. The OPAL Soil Centre ran that OPAL Soil and Earthworm Survey. It is one of five centres of expertise of the Open Air Laboratories Network, based at the Centre for Environmental Policy, Imperial College London. Volunteers collected habitat and soil information and identified earthworms. Results were analysed to study soil and earthworm distribution across England and the effects humans have on soils. Its aims include community-level information on soil quality and biodiversity, and research on pollution sources and pathways in soil.

soil-hist-143.title: Central Soil Salinity Research Institute
soil-hist-143.text: The institute is an autonomous Indian body under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, devoted to salt-affected soils. It began at Hisar in 1969 after an Indo-American team's water management recommendations, and moved to Karnal that year. Four divisions cover soil and crop management, irrigation and drainage engineering, crop improvement and social science. The engineers work on groundwater recharge and subsurface drainage of waterlogged saline soils. Crop improvement breeds saline- and alkali-tolerant rice, wheat and mustard. The institute also coordinates the national project on managing salt-affected soils and using saline water.

soil-hist-142.title: Indian Institute of Soil Science
soil-hist-142.text: Founded in 1988 at Bhopal, this autonomous institute under the Indian Council of Agricultural Research was set up for advanced research in {{ref:soil-found-090}}. It covers coordinated projects on soil test crop response (17 centres), micronutrients and biofertilizers (11 centres each). Six divisions include soil physics, soil chemistry and fertility, soil biology and environmental soil science. It trains in soil testing, nutrient and water efficiency, carbon sequestration and soil quality assessment. Its mandate covers research on soil physical, chemical and biological processes and environment-friendly management technologies. A long-term fertilizer experiments project studies fertilizer effects on productivity and soil quality.

soil-hist-141.title: Heath: shrubland on poor, acid ground
soil-hist-141.text:
Heath is what grows where soil gives little. It is a shrubland habitat found mainly on free-draining, infertile, acidic soils, with open, low-growing woody vegetation. Heathland is favoured by hard, dry climates, especially in summer, and by acidic, low-fertility, often sandy soils. A small mire may form where drainage is poor. Heaths are dominated by low shrubs 20 cm to 2 m tall. They range from very species-rich in Australia and South African fynbos to depauperate in Europe, where heather, heath and gorse dominate.

Many heaths are anthropogenic, made by centuries of clearing woodland by grazing and burning. They are kept by grazing and periodic burning (swailing) or rarely mowing, or they are recolonised by woodland. Heaths are widespread but rapidly disappearing and rare in Europe. Tree incursion after traditional management stopped, and urban sprawl, threaten them.

soil-hist-154.title: National Society of Consulting Soil Scientists
soil-hist-154.text: This North American professional society of soil scientists, mainly environmental consultants, merged into the Soil Science Society of America (SSSA) in August 2011. Its members worked on topics such as {{ref:soil-fert-192}}, {{ref:soil-agri-169}}, {{ref:soil-water-124}}, {{ref:soil-water-002}} and {{ref:soil-env-062}}. It awarded the Registered Professional Soil Scientist (RPSS) designation in the United States and stressed professional ethics in certification. It became an SSSA chapter in 1996, a cooperator of the National Cooperative Soil Survey in 1997, and was a member of the International Union of Soil Sciences. In 2011 the SSSA board created Division S12 for Consulting Soil Scientists, and 95% of NSCSS members voted to integrate. SSSA's corporate umbrella and Science Policy Office were cited as advantages.
